summary: This unit teaches you to keep a housekeeping store secure and clean. You will learn why stores are locked and who may enter, how keys, visitors and issuing are controlled, how counts and records show theft early, how to keep a store free of pests, damp and mould, how to arrange stock, chemicals and linen safely, how to prevent fire and injury, how to clean the store on a schedule, and how to close and secure it.

blocks.p: The housekeeping store holds linen, guest amenities, paper goods, chemicals and equipment worth hundreds of thousands of Jamaican dollars. It is where the department's supplies wait until they are needed. If it is left open, stock is stolen or misused. If it is dirty or damp, linen is spoiled, pests move in and people get hurt. **Security and cleanliness** protect the money, the guests and the staff.
This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees. It applies to the main housekeeping store of a hotel, a floor store, and the small store room of a villa.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks: deep cleaning and reorganising a store, and a security check with a spot count, role plays and a closing procedure. The assessor looks at your method, safety, honesty, records and teamwork.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A store is locked when no one is working in it, **to prevent theft and misuse**. Valuable, portable items such as towels, toiletries, irons, hair dryers, kettles and spare televisions are easy to carry away. Chemicals can be misused or may hurt someone who does not know the dangers.

ul: **Authorised persons only**: the storekeeper, housekeeping supervisor and staff the supervisor has approved.
Visitors and contractors **sign in, state the reason, and are accompanied** all the time they are in the store, then sign out.
Staff keep personal bags, lunch and coats **outside** the store.
If you do not know a person, politely ask if you can help; if unsure, call the supervisor or security.

head: Rule
Why
rows: Keys are kept by named people and signed out and in on a **key log**
The log shows who had the key at any time
Hand a key to the next person yourself and sign it over, never leave it
A key left in a door or on a hook can be copied or taken
Never lend your key or copy it
Copies are impossible to track
If you leave the store for even ten minutes, lock it and take the key
An open store is open to anyone
A lost key is reported at once
Locks may need to be changed
Spare keys are kept locked in a key box
A spare on a nail or in a drawer is no security

head: Measure
How it helps
rows: Strong door, good lock and shutters or burglar bars on windows
Make a break-in hard
CCTV or an alarm
A camera at the entrance records who goes in; an alarm gives warning
Lighting outside
Intruders are easier to see
A locked cage or cabinet inside the store
Keeps high-value items (irons, hair dryers, spare kettles) extra safe
Visitor log
Shows who came in, when and why
Spot checks by the supervisor
Show real stock and discourage theft

blocks.note: A store that has a CCTV camera still needs locks, keys and records. A camera records what happens: it does not stop a theft by itself.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Stock leaves the store **only against a signed requisition** from an authorised person. This way every issue is approved and recorded, and the record shows where the stock went.

flow: Receive the written requisition
Check that it is signed by an authorised person
Check what is asked is reasonable
Pick, count and hand over the stock
Both people check and sign the issue sheet
Update the stock card the same day

blocks.p: If a request is not signed, **refuse politely**: 'I am sorry, I need a signed requisition. Please ask your supervisor to sign it, and I will give it to you straight away.' Do not make exceptions for friends or for busy times.

ul: Watch the delivery until all of it is put away; do not leave goods in a corridor or an open doorway.
Count, check and sign for the quantity actually received.
Put new stock in the right place, behind the old (first in, first out).

blocks.p: Stock is counted regularly and the supervisor also does **spot checks**: a count of a few items, with no warning. The count is compared with the stock record.

head: Item
Record
Count
Difference
rows: Hand towels
4 missing
Toilet rolls
None
Soap bars
12 more than the record

flow: Recount the item
Check issue sheets, requisitions and deliveries not yet entered
Check for damage or waste not recorded
Write up the difference
Report it to the supervisor
Do not accuse anyone

blocks.note: Records are protected too: do not leave stock cards or stock records open on a counter. Someone could change them to hide a theft.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: If you suspect theft or a break-in

head: Situation
What to do
rows: Shortages keep appearing and you cannot explain them
Report the facts and the pattern (days, items, shifts) to the supervisor; do not accuse anyone
You see a co-worker taking store items for herself
Do not confront her; report what you saw to your supervisor
The door or lock looks forced, or the store is open when it should be shut
Do not go in or touch anything; keep others away; tell security and the supervisor at once
The lock is broken
Report it at once and keep the store watched until it is repaired

blocks.note: Do not touch or move anything at a break-in. The police may need to examine the scene. Write down what you saw and the time.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Sign
Likely pest
What it means
rows: Small dark droppings, gnaw marks, torn packs
Rats or mice (rodents)
Food, paper or soap packs are being eaten; disease risk
Live or dead cockroaches, egg cases, dark spots
Cockroaches
Moist, dirty places; they spread germs
Trails of ants to a spilled item
Ants
A sweet or greasy spill; clean it
Small holes in cloth or paper
Moths, silverfish and other insects
Stored cloth or paper is being damaged

ul: Keep the store **clean and dry**, with no crumbs, spills or rubbish.
**No eating or drinking** in the store: crumbs and spills attract pests.
Keep doors closed and **seal gaps** around pipes, doors and walls.
Leave a gap between shelves and the wall so you can clean and inspect.
Take empty cardboard boxes out quickly: pests hide in them and they burn easily.
Store stock on shelves or pallets, **off the floor**.
Take rubbish out daily; keep bins covered.

blocks.note: If you see signs of pests, report them to your supervisor. Pest control is done by a trained contractor with approved products. Do not spray strong pesticides yourself or put out poison where linen and amenities are kept.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Ventilation** is the flow of fresh air through a room. Jamaica is hot and humid and the rainy seasons bring a lot of damp. Poor ventilation causes damp air, and damp stock is damaged stock.

head: Problem
Effect on stock
What to do
rows: Damp air and leaks
**Mould**: black, grey or green spots and a musty smell on linen, paper and cardboard
Fix leaks; open vents or use fans; keep stock off the floor and away from walls; report the cause
Heat
Some products spoil, melt or become unsafe (lotions, some chemicals, batteries)
Keep the store cool and out of direct sun; keep products away from heaters and roofs
Poor air flow
Stuffy air and smells
Open vents, keep gaps between stacks
Standing water on the floor
Slips and damp
Dry it; find the source

blocks.note: Mouldy linen and paper must be set aside and reported. Do not use mouldy linen for guests. Wear gloves and a mask if there is a lot of mould.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Arranging stock and keeping the store safe

head: Stock
Where and how
rows: Chemicals
**Low down**, in labelled containers, closed
**Apart** from linen and guest amenities
Strong acids and bleach **apart** from each other
Concentrates behind a locked door where possible
Clean linen
On shelves, covered, off the floor
Never beside soiled linen, rubbish or chemicals
Guest amenities and paper goods
Clean, dry shelves; off the floor
Away from chemicals and damp
High-value items
In a locked cage or cabinet
Equipment
Clean, dry, in its place; faulty items tagged 'Do not use'

blocks.p: Label every shelf and bin so stock is kept in its place. Put the **oldest stock at the front** and new stock behind it, so nothing goes out of date. Stock that has been pushed to the back and gone out of date shows that old stock is not used first.

ul: Make **stable stacks**; put heavy items low and light items high.
Do not stack higher than is safe, and do not stack right up to the ceiling or sprinkler heads: it can block the sprinklers and the stack can fall.
Keep aisles **clear** so that nobody trips and everyone can get out quickly.
Never stand on a shelf or a box to reach stock. Use a **step stool** or safe ladder.
Lift correctly: bend your knees, keep your back straight, hold the load close.
Keep **exits clear** and an **extinguisher** near the door, in date and easy to reach.
Remove empty cardboard and rubbish quickly: they burn easily.
Do not overload sockets or leave cables trailing. A light fitting that flickers or smells of burning: switch off if it is safe, keep clear and report it.
Keep flammable products (some polishes and solvents) away from heat.
Know your property's fire plan: where the alarm and assembly point are. In Jamaica, the emergency number for the fire brigade and ambulance is 110 and for the police 119.

flow: Put out a wet floor sign and keep people away
Wear gloves, eye protection and closed shoes
Read the label or SDS
Contain and soak up the spill with the spill kit
Clean the area and dispose of the waste as the SDS says
Report it and replace the spill kit

blocks.note: Strong acid cleaner and bleach must be kept apart. If they leak and mix, a toxic gas forms. If you smell gas, leave at once, raise the alarm and do not go back in.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Good lighting lets you read labels and see hazards. Replace blown bulbs promptly.
Keep the floor dry and free of boxes.
Broken glass: wrap it in thick paper, put it in a marked container, and do not pick it up with bare hands.

blocks.p: Closed non-slip shoes, gloves, and eye protection when handling chemicals or cleaning high shelves.

A **cleaning schedule** is a plan that lists what is cleaned in the store, how often and by whom. For example: floor swept daily; shelves wiped weekly; deep clean every four weeks (that is, every 28 days) or as the property decides. A **checklist** is signed and dated each time, so it shows what was cleaned, when and by whom.

flow: Wear PPE and read the labels
Walk through and note hazards, pests, damp and damaged stock
Move the stock on the shelf aside (or to a clean trolley)
Dust the shelves and ledges from top to bottom
Wipe with detergent, then disinfect if the schedule says so
Let it dry, then put stock back in order
Sweep and mop the floor from the back towards the door, with a wet floor sign out
Take out cardboard and waste; clean and store equipment
Complete and sign the checklist

head: Rule
Reason
rows: Top to bottom
Dust falls on lower surfaces you have not cleaned yet
Dry before wet
Sweep or dust first, so dirt does not turn to mud
Back to the door
You do not walk on a floor you have just cleaned
Shelves before the floor
Dust and dirt fall to the floor
Move stock aside, then replace in order
The shelf is cleaned underneath; stock is not mixed up
Clean first, then disinfect
Disinfectant does not work on dirt

blocks.p: After the shelves are clean, put the stock back with the **oldest at the front**, heavy items low, chemicals low and apart from linen and amenities, and every shelf labelled. Set aside damaged and out-of-date items and record them.

blocks.h: Keeping it clean day to day

ul: Tidy as you work: no boxes in the aisle; no spills left.
Clean up spills at once.
Take rubbish out daily; keep bins covered.
Keep clean and soiled linen apart; clean linen is not stored near rubbish.
Wash and dry cleaning equipment after use and store it in its place.

blocks.note: A deep clean every 10 days gives 3 deep cleans in 30 days: schedules make the work predictable, and a signed checklist proves it was done.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The supervisor inspects the store regularly to check that it is clean, safe and secure. Be ready for it: have the checklist signed, the stock in order and the key log up to date.

flow: Collect the key and sign the key log
Check the door and lock for signs of forcing
Switch on the light and check the floor and shelves
Check for leaks, pests and smells
Compare the visible stock with yesterday's closing note
Report anything unusual before you start work
Check all areas, including behind doors
Put away stock and equipment; tidy the aisles
Lock the cage or cabinet
Switch off lights, fans and electrical items
Close and lock windows and shutters
Lock the door and test it
Sign the key log and hand the key to the right person
Write the closing note and sign the checklist

blocks.note: Check that there is nobody inside and no equipment left on before you lock. Sign the key in with the evening supervisor, not on the desk or in a drawer.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Write a short report: what you checked, what you found (hazards, shortages, damage, pests, damp), and at least three recommendations, for example: 'Fit a stronger lock on the window; move chemicals to the bottom shelf; clear the aisle by the exit.' Use facts only, with dates and times.

sections.title: Handling linen, amenities and chemicals in the store

blocks.p: Different kinds of stock need different care. Mixing them up is one of the most common ways a store becomes unsafe or unclean.

ul: Clean linen is kept on shelves, covered, **off the floor and away from walls**, in a dry place.
Soiled linen goes straight to the laundry in a closed bag. It is never kept in the store with clean linen, amenities or rubbish.
Rotate the stock: use the oldest clean linen first, so no pile sits unused for months and goes yellow or mouldy.
Check linen when it comes back from the laundry for stains, tears and damp. Set aside damaged items and record them.
Count linen at set times and compare with the record. Linen is a common item for loss.
Keep them in their packs on clean, dry shelves, off the floor and away from chemicals.
Toilet rolls and tissue absorb damp and smells. Soap, lotions and shampoos can leak or melt in heat.
Do not open cartons you do not need yet. An opened carton is easy to take from and easy for pests to enter.
Check expiry dates on lotions and similar products and use the oldest first.

head: Do
Do not
rows: Keep them in their original labelled containers, closed
Pour them into drink bottles or unlabelled bottles
Store them low down, apart from linen and amenities
Store them above linen or beside food
Keep acids and bleach apart
Store acid cleaner and bleach on the same shelf
Keep an SDS for each product where staff can find it
Guess what an unlabelled bottle contains
Keep a spill kit near the chemical shelf
Mix chemicals to make them stronger

blocks.p: Heat and sunlight can spoil some chemicals and make containers unsafe, so the store must not get very hot.

blocks.note: A bottle without a label is never used. Tell the supervisor and have it identified or disposed of safely.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Check cables and plugs on vacuum cleaners, irons and floor machines before they are issued and when they are returned.
A faulty item is tagged **Do not use** and reported. It is kept apart from working equipment.
Return equipment clean and dry. Mops hung wet grow germs and smell.
Record who takes out equipment such as irons and kettles, and when they bring it back.

sections.title: Incidents, reporting and working with others

blocks.p: Even in a well-run store things go wrong. Your job is to deal with the immediate danger safely, record what happened and tell the right person.

head: Incident
First action
Then
rows: A person is hurt (cut, fall, strain)
Give first aid if you are trained; call the first aider or supervisor
Fill in the accident report as soon as possible
Chemical on skin or in eyes
Rinse at once with plenty of clean running water
Get medical help; report and record it
Small fire or smoke
Raise the alarm and follow the fire plan; use the extinguisher only if it is safe and you are trained
Report it, even if it is out
Flooding or a leak
Move stock away if safe; put out a sign; switch off electrical items if safe
Report it so it can be repaired
Signs of a break-in
Do not enter or touch anything
Tell security and the supervisor; write down what you saw and the time
Hurricane warning
Follow the property's hurricane plan: move stock off the floor and away from windows, secure doors, check the store
Report what has been done

ol: Say **when** (date and time) and **where** (which store, which shelf or door).
Say **what** you saw or found, using facts: 'two packs of toilet rolls with gnaw marks', not 'rats everywhere'.
Say **what you did** (put out a sign, locked the door, moved stock).
Give your name and sign it.
Add suggestions where you can: what would stop it happening again.

ul: Share the work fairly when cleaning: each person takes a bay or section.
Check each other's counts and sums.
Share security duties at changeover: tell the next person about anything unusual.
Be honest. Report your own mistakes, such as stock dropped and broken, quickly. Hiding a mistake costs the property more.

blocks.note: Security and cleanliness are everybody's job. A store that is only clean when the supervisor is expected, or only locked when someone remembers, is not a secure and clean store.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: I can explain why a store is locked and who may enter.
I can control keys, visitors and contractors.
I can issue stock only against a signed requisition and refuse an unsigned one politely.
I can count stock, compare it with the records, recount and report a difference.
I can say what to do if I suspect theft or find a forced door.
I can spot the signs of rats, mice, cockroaches and ants and say how to prevent them.
I can explain how damp, heat and poor ventilation damage stock and what to do about them.
I can arrange chemicals, linen, amenities and high-value items correctly, oldest at the front.
I can stack safely and keep aisles and exits clear.
I can say how to prevent fire in a store and what to do about a spill.
I can clean a store in the right order and complete the checklist.
I can open, close and secure the store.
I can handle linen, amenities, chemicals and equipment in the store correctly.
I can deal with an incident and write a short report with recommendations.

terms: A person who has been given permission to enter the store.
A record of who holds each key and when.
A written request for stock, signed by an authorised person.
A count of a few items made without warning.
Closed-circuit television: cameras that record an area.
A locked metal-mesh enclosure for high-value items.
Black, grey or green growth on damp linen, paper and cardboard.
The flow of fresh air through a room.
A plan listing what is cleaned, how often and by whom.
A kit with absorbent pads and gloves for cleaning up a chemical leak.
A safe small ladder or stool for reaching high shelves.

c1.title: Closing the store at a Montego Bay resort
c1.text: At a resort in Montego Bay, storekeeper Winston is about to close the housekeeping store at 6:00 p.m. The store has a steel door, a window with louvres, a locked cage for irons and kettles, and a CCTV camera at the door. A set of spare keys hangs on a nail inside the door. The evening supervisor, Mrs. Bailey, is on her way from the other end of the property to collect the key.

c2.title: Damp and droppings in a Black River store
c2.text: During the rainy season at a guest house in Black River, storekeeper Janelle opens the housekeeping store and notices a musty smell. A cardboard box of bath towels on the floor by the back wall is dark and damp, with black spots on the towels. Small dark droppings and a gnawed corner of a bar-soap pack are on the bottom shelf. A leak in the roof has dripped onto the floor, and a half-eaten mango has been left on a shelf by a cleaner.

c3.title: Shortages in an Ocho Rios store
c3.text: At a hotel in Ocho Rios, supervisor Mr. Edwards finds that bath towel stock has been short by about 12 towels at the last three weekly counts. Each shortage was found after the weekend, when only one storekeeper, Andre, has been on duty. A visitor log is kept but is often not signed on weekends. On Monday a trainee, Shelly, tells him quietly that she saw a cleaner put a pack of soap in her bag on Saturday.

c4.title: Boxes and wires in a May Pen store
c4.text: In a small hotel in May Pen, a safety check of the housekeeping store finds cartons stacked from floor to ceiling directly under the sprinkler heads. The aisle between the shelves is half blocked by empty boxes. A cleaning-product bottle has leaked on a shelf, and a light fitting flickers and smells of burning. The only fire extinguisher is on the floor behind a stack of boxes.

c5.title: Deep-cleaning day at a Portmore store
c5.text: On deep-cleaning day at a hotel in Portmore, the storekeeper team has four bays to clean in the housekeeping store. Each bay holds linen, paper goods, amenities and chemicals. The cleaning schedule says a deep clean is done every 10 days, and the checklist must be signed after each. The team has gloves, a mop, two buckets, wet floor signs, disinfectant and cloths.

questions.q: A friend who works at another property calls at the store and asks to look inside 'just to see it'. What should Winston do?
o: Politely refuse: authorised people only
Let her in for a minute, if he stays beside her
Let her in if she signs the visitor log first
Let her in if she leaves her bag outside the door
questions.why: Only authorised people, or visitors with a work reason who are signed in and accompanied, may enter. A friend's curiosity is not a work reason, and a polite refusal protects both of them.

questions.q: How should Winston hand the key to Mrs. Bailey?
o: Leave it in the office drawer for her to collect
Give it to the security guard to pass on to her
Hang it on the nail with the spare keys for her
Hand it to her and both sign the key log
questions.why: A key is passed from hand to hand and signed over, so the log shows who held it at any time. A key left in a drawer or on a nail cannot be traced.

questions.q: What is wrong with the spare keys hanging on a nail inside the store door?
o: The nail may wear out and the keys fall on the floor
Spare keys should hang outside so staff can reach them
Anyone who gets in can take them; use a key box
Spare keys are not needed when a store has a camera
questions.why: Spare keys are as valuable as the main key. They are kept in a locked key box and their use is logged.

questions.q: Before locking up, which check is part of securing this store?
o: Switching off the camera at the door to save power
Checking the window is shut and the cage locked
Leaving the louvres open so that the air can circulate
Leaving the cage open so staff can reach the irons
questions.why: A closing check covers the door, windows, cage, lights and electrical items. A window left open is a way in even when the door is locked.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the black spots on the towels?
o: Mould, from damp cardboard against the wall
Ink that has run from the printing on the cardboard
Dye running out of the new towels when they got wet
Dust blown in from the cracks in the roof above them
questions.why: Damp air and wet cardboard let mould grow on cloth. The roof leak and floor storage made it worse.

questions.q: What should Janelle do with the mouldy towels?
o: Dry them in the sun, then use them in the rooms as normal
Spray them with air freshener and put them back on the shelf
Wash them with the others and not mention the mould
Set them aside and report them, not use them for guests
questions.why: Mouldy linen can affect health and spoils the guest's stay. Remove it, record it and report the cause, which is the leak.

questions.q: What do the small dark droppings and the gnawed soap pack suggest?
o: A careless cleaner has dropped and torn the soap pack
The soap arrived damaged from the supplier's van
Rats or mice; report it for pest control
Cockroaches have been eating the bar soap for weeks
questions.why: Small dark droppings and gnaw marks are signs of rodents. Report them so a trained contractor can deal with them, and check how they are getting in.

questions.q: What does the half-eaten mango on the shelf show about store rules?
o: Staff may eat in the store if they sweep up afterwards
Food attracts pests, so none may be kept in the store
Fruit is allowed because it is natural and not packaged
Food is allowed on the top shelf but not on the floor
questions.why: No eating or drinking in the store: crumbs, peel and spills attract rats, cockroaches and ants.

questions.q: What should Mr. Edwards do first about the repeated shortages?
o: Check the records and the pattern, not accuse anyone
Dismiss Andre at once, because he works the weekends
Tell the whole team that the shortages are Andre's fault
Order extra towels and say nothing to anyone about it
questions.why: Repeated shortages need investigation. The pattern points to weak control, but accusing someone without facts is unfair and may be wrong.

questions.q: Which change would best reduce the chance of theft on weekends?
o: Leave the store door open so that staff can help themselves
Move all the towels to the floor pantry on Fridays
Count the stock only once a year, after the busy season
Make visitors sign the log and add a second count
questions.why: A visitor log that is really filled in, plus extra checks, makes weekend theft easier to see and harder to hide.

questions.q: What should Shelly do about the soap she saw going into the bag?
o: Confront the cleaner herself in front of the others
Tell her friends in the laundry what she saw
Report exactly what she saw to her supervisor
Say nothing, as it is only one pack of soap
questions.why: Staff report theft through the proper channel, with facts, without confronting or gossiping. Small repeated thefts add up to a large loss.

questions.q: The weekend count is 12 towels below the stock card. What should Mr. Edwards check before treating it as theft?
o: Check only the towels that are in the laundry room
Recount, then look for unrecorded issues and returns
Ask each cleaner to say who might have taken them
Write the difference off in the record straight away
questions.why: A difference can come from a counting error or from movements that were not written down. Recount and check the paperwork first.

questions.q: Why is stacking cartons up to the sprinkler heads a problem?
o: It can block the spray, and tall stacks can fall
It makes the cartons too warm for the stock inside
It lets pests climb up to the ceiling more easily
It hides the lights so staff cannot read the labels
questions.why: Sprinklers need clear space to spread water. Tall, unstable stacks can also fall and injure staff.

questions.q: What is the right action for the flickering light that smells of burning?
o: Change the bulb and carry on with the stock count
Wrap tape around the fitting and leave it for now
Leave it until the electrician's next planned visit
Switch off if safe, keep clear and report it
questions.why: A burning smell can mean overheating wires or a fire starting. Switch off if it is safe, keep away and report it at once.

questions.q: What is wrong with the extinguisher standing on the floor behind boxes?
o: It should be hidden so that nobody can steal it
It should be on the top shelf where children cannot reach
It must be in view and easy to reach, near the exit
It should be locked in a cabinet to keep it safe
questions.why: An extinguisher is only useful if it can be reached in seconds. Keep it near the exit, clear of stock, in date and checked.

questions.q: A bottle of cleaner has leaked on a shelf. What should be done first?
o: Mop the shelf at once with a wet cloth and bare hands
Put on gloves and eye protection, then follow the SDS
Move the bottle into a drawer and clean it up later
Pour water over the shelf and leave it to run off
questions.why: Wear PPE, read the label or SDS, then contain and clean the spill with the spill kit. Never improvise with water or other products.

questions.q: In what order should each team member clean a bay?
o: Stock aside, dust top to bottom, wipe, then restock
Mop the floor first, then wipe the shelves above it
Wipe the lowest shelf first and the top shelf last
Put the stock back first, then dust around it
questions.why: Moving stock aside lets you clean the whole shelf. Work top to bottom so that dust falls on surfaces still to be cleaned, and do the floor last.

questions.q: How many deep cleans does the schedule give in 30 days?
questions.why: 30 days / 10 days = 3 deep cleans.

questions.q: When the stock goes back, how should it be arranged?
o: Newest at the front, so it is easy to see and use
Chemicals on the top shelf, above the clean linen
Oldest at the front, heavy and chemicals low
The heaviest cartons on the highest shelf
questions.why: Using the oldest stock first prevents waste. Heavy items and chemicals go low so they cannot fall, and chemicals stay apart from linen and amenities.

questions.q: Why is the checklist signed and dated after each deep clean?
o: It lets the team skip the next scheduled clean
It shows what was cleaned, when and by whom
It proves that the store has no pests in it
It replaces the supervisor's regular inspection
questions.why: A signed, dated checklist is a record that the work was done and who did it, which the supervisor can check.
